subject: Banking
title: The Death of the Bank Branch
description: A quick, practical guide to The Death of the Bank Branch.

hook.text: US banks have closed 12,000 branches since 2009. One in five bank branches has disappeared in just 15 years.

buildup.text: Online and mobile banking replaced most branch visits. Deposits, transfers, and bill payments happen on phones now.

discovery.text: Each branch costs $2-4 million per year to run. Closing one saves millions while barely affecting customer satisfaction.

twist.text: Branch closures hit rural and low-income areas hardest.

climax.text: Branches are dying because digital is cheaper. But not everyone is digital.

punchline.text: 12,000 branches closed. Digital is cheaper. But banking deserts are growing.

quiz.question: How many US bank branches have closed since 2009?

details.summary: Banks have closed over 15,000 US branches since 2009 as digital banking removes the need for physical locations. Branch closures disproportionately affect rural communities and elderly customers who depend on in-person services.
details.whyItMatters: Branch closures save banks billions but create banking deserts where entire communities lose access to financial services. The equity implications of digital-only banking remain a critical policy challenge.
takeaways: Over 15,000 US bank branches closed between 2009 and 2023
Rural and low-income areas are disproportionately affected by closures
A single branch closure can reduce local small business lending significantly

faq.question: Who is most affected by bank branch closures?
faq.answer: Elderly customers who are less comfortable with technology, rural communities without reliable internet, small businesses that depend on cash handling services, and low-income populations who use in-person services for check cashing and financial questions.

faq.question: Can digital banking fully replace physical branches?
faq.answer: For most routine transactions, yes. But complex services like notarization, safe deposit boxes, large cash handling, and face-to-face advisory for major financial decisions still require physical presence that digital cannot fully replicate.
